The '''1935 Canadian federal election''' was held on October 14, 1935, to elect members of the [[House of Commons of Canada]] of the [[18th Canadian Parliament|18th Parliament]] of [[Canada]]. The [[Liberal Party of Canada|Liberal Party]] of [[William Lyon Mackenzie King]] won a [[majority government]], defeating [[Prime Minister of Canada|Prime Minister]] [[R. B. Bennett]]'s [[Conservative Party of Canada (1867-1942)|Conservatives]].<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Reid|first=Escott|date=1936|title=The Canadian Election of 1935—and After|url=https://www.cambridge.org/core/product/identifier/S0003055400030914/type/journal_article|journal=American Political Science Review|language=en|volume=30|issue=1|pages=111–121|doi=10.2307/1948012|jstor=1948012 |s2cid=147100835 |issn=0003-0554|url-access=subscription}}</ref>

The central issue was the economy, which was still in the depths of the [[Canada in the Great Depression|Great Depression]]. In office since the [[1930 Canadian federal election|1930 election]], Bennett had sought to stimulate the economy during his first few years through a policy of high tariffs and trade within the [[British Empire]]. In the last months of his time in office, he reversed his position, copying the popular [[New Deal]] of [[Franklin D. Roosevelt|Franklin Roosevelt]] in the [[United States]]. Upset about high unemployment and inaction by the federal government, voters were unwilling to allow the Conservatives to continue to govern, despite their change of policy.

The Conservatives were also suffering severe internal divisions. During his first years in office, Bennett had alienated those in his party who supported intervention in the economy. His last minute conversion to interventionism alienated the rest of the party. Former cabinet minister [[H.H. Stevens]] left to form the [[Reconstruction Party of Canada|Reconstruction Party]]. Senior minister Sir [[Joseph Flavelle]] announced he would be supporting the Liberals.

Support for Bennett's Tories dropped by a third and 20 percentage points. And their drop in seats was worse. Conservatives took just 39 seats, which was the party's smallest ever seat count until their collapse in [[1993 Canadian federal election|1993]]. 

Mackenzie King promised mild reforms to restore economic health. The Liberals received a small increase in votes compared to 1930 but took many more seats this time, taking 173 seats to the Conservatives' 39. The Liberal Party would continue to hold power until 1957.

The 1935 election was also important in that it saw the final demise of the [[Progressive Party of Canada|Progressive Party]] and the [[United Farmers of Alberta]]. The Progressive Party, having been in decline over the previous decade, did not run any candidates under its own banner. The federal party, always highly decentralized, ceased to exist sometime circa 1940. However, [[Liberal-Progressive]] Premier of Manitoba [[John Bracken]] brought the name back into formal use when he moved to federal politics and the Conservative Party in 1942, winning the leadership [[1942 Progressive Conservative leadership convention]]. His first act as Conservative Party leader was to rechristen them the [[Progressive Conservative Party of Canada|Progressive Conservative Party]].

The United Farmers of Alberta, whose credibility was ruined by a sex scandal involving premier [[John Edward Brownlee|John E. Brownlee]], had lost all their seats in the [[1935 Alberta general election|provincial election]] earlier that year due to the popularity of the Social Credit. The UFA had signed on to the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation party, founded in 1932, and again suffering under shadow of the Social Credit wave, elected no MPs in this federal election. The eight sitting MPs such as Michael Luchkovich were no more successful than new faces in this regard. 

Two new movements rose out of the west, however. The new [[Co-operative Commonwealth Federation]], a [[social democratic]] party, first competed in this election and won seven seats (including [[Tommy Douglas]]' first stint in elective office), promising social reform. The [[Social Credit Party of Canada]] was even more successful, capturing seventeen seats on its platform of monetary reform despite winning less of the popular vote than the former. Fifteen of these seats were in [[Alberta]], where the party dominated after having swept to power in a landslide less than two months before the federal vote. [[John Horne Blackmore]] was chosen to lead the Social Credit caucus after the election. The de facto leader of the national movement was Alberta Premier [[William Aberhart]], who did not stand in the federal election himself.
